property_summary: For any inputs to initialize, the correct contract sets its public baseToken to the _baseToken argument passed (i.e. c.baseToken() == _baseToken after initialize returns); the mutant unconditionally sets baseToken = address(0) and therefore will violate this for any call where _baseToken != address(0).

For any inputs to initialize, the contract's public baseToken equals the _baseToken argument passed (i.e., initialize sets baseToken to the provided _baseToken); the mutant breaks this because it sets baseToken = msg.sender instead.

For any inputs to initialize, the reference contract sets baseToken equal to the _baseToken parameter (i.e. c.baseToken() == _baseToken) while the mutant that swaps assignments will make c.baseToken() != _baseToken for some inputs; thus the invariant is: after initialize(...) returns successfully, c.baseToken() equals the provided _baseToken argument.

For any inputs to initialize, the reference contract always sets its public nft state variable to the _nft parameter (so c.nft() == _nft after initialize returns), whereas the mutant that omits assigning nft will leave c.nft() unchanged for some inputs (so there exist inputs where c.nft() != _nft).

For any inputs to initialize, the reference contract stores the provided _nft address into the public nft() getter (i.e. c.nft() == _nft after initialize returns); the mutant sets nft to address(0) instead, so there exist inputs where c.nft() != _nft and the property is violated.
For any inputs to initialize, the reference contract stores changeFee exactly equal to the provided _changeFee; the mutant increments the provided _changeFee by 1 so this equality can be violated.

For any initialize inputs, the contract's stored changeFee equals the _changeFee argument passed to initialize (i.e. changeFee == _changeFee); the mutant that decrements the stored value breaks this invariant for some inputs.

For any inputs to initialize, the contract stores the provided _changeFee into the public changeFee state variable (i.e. c.changeFee() == _changeFee); the mutant sets changeFee to 0 instead, so it violates this when _changeFee != 0.

For any inputs to initialize, the reference contract always stores the provided _changeFee into the public changeFee state variable; the mutant that omits assigning changeFee leaves it at zero for some inputs (when _changeFee != 0) and thus violates this property.

For all inputs, calling initialize(...) on the correct contract reverts if _feeRate > 5000 (so feeRate on-chain is never > 5000 after initialize), whereas the mutant accepts any _feeRate allowing feeRate > 5000 for some inputs.

For any inputs to initialize, the deployed C contract sets its public feeRate to the provided _feeRate (subject to the existing validation) — the mutant that clamps feeRate to 0 causes feeRate() to differ from the supplied value for some fuzzed _feeRate inputs.

For every admissible initialize(...) input where _feeRate is <= 5000, the reference contract never reverts and after initialize completes feeRate == _feeRate; the mutant, which assigns feeRate before checking the cap, can transiently set feeRate to an out-of-range value causing observable difference when initialize is invoked with _feeRate > 5000 (mutant reverts but leaves feeRate set) — thus the invariant 'if initialize reverts then feeRate remains unchanged (zero)' holds for reference but can be violated by the mutant for some inputs.

For any call to initialize(...), if the call reverts then the contract's feeRate remains unchanged (i.e. still 0 for a fresh contract); the mutant can leave feeRate set even when initialize reverts, violating this invariant for some inputs.

For any inputs to initialize, if the call reverts then the contract's stored feeRate remains its pre-initialize value (fresh contract => 0); the mutant that assigns feeRate before checking the cap can leave feeRate changed despite revert, violating this rule for some fuzzed _feeRate > 5000.

For any fuzzed _feeRate and other initialize parameters, if initialize(...) reverts then the contract's public feeRate getter returns its pre-call value (for a fresh contract that is 0); the mutant that assigns feeRate before validating the cap can leave feeRate changed even when initialize reverts, violating this property for some inputs.

For any fuzzed initialize(...) inputs, if initialize completes successfully then c.feeRate() equals the provided _feeRate; the mutant (which assigns feeRate before validating the cap) can cause a revert on too-large _feeRate but nevertheless leave feeRate set (so there exists an input where initialize reverts yet feeRate != pre-call value), therefore the reference guarantees that a successful initialize sets feeRate to the argument and no partial assignment remains on revert while the mutant can violate that by leaving feeRate modified when initialize reverts.

For any input parameters, calling initialize on a fresh C instance twice in a row must revert on the second call (reference enforces this by reverting if already initialized); the mutant removes that revert, allowing the second initialize to succeed and potentially change state.

For any input arguments, the first call to initialize(...) on a fresh C contract must succeed and set initialized == true; the mutant inverts the check causing initialize to revert on first call (or never set initialized), so for some inputs the mutant leaves initialized == false while the reference sets it true.

For any input parameters, the reference contract's first call to initialize(...) succeeds and results in c.initialized() == true; the mutant inverts the initialized check causing initialize to revert on first call and leave initialized == false for some inputs.

For any input parameters, calling initialize(...) on a fresh C contract should succeed (not revert) and leave initialized == true; the mutant inverts the initialized check causing initialize to revert on first call and therefore initialized remains false.

For any fuzzed initialization parameters, the first call to initialize(...) on a fresh C contract MUST succeed (not revert) and set c.initialized() == true; the mutant inverts the precondition causing the first initialize call to revert (or leave initialized == false) for some inputs.
